title: The Benefits of Daylight through Windows
authors: Peter Boyce, Claudia Hunter and Owen Howlett, 2003
review_question: To identify the impacts of daylight on human performance and workplace productivity, human health, and financial return on investment in work-related buildings, and to identify what is known and not known about these impacts.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Impacts of daylight reviewed for buildings used for work (offices, schools, hospitals, retail stores) where daylighting has been extensively studied. Daylight in housing is not considered.

findings.quote: Electric light sources can be constructed to closely match a spectrum of daylight, but none have been made that mimic the variation in light spectrum that occurs with daylight at different times, in different seasons, and under different weather conditions.

findings.consequent: Human visual system, human circadian system
findings.quote: Physiologically, daylight is an effective stimulant to the human visual system and the human circadian system.
Psychologically, daylight and a view are much desired.

Daylight does have a greater probability of maximizing visual performance than most forms of electric lighting because it tends to be delivered in large amounts with a spectrum that ensures excellent color rendering.

findings.antecedent: Poorly delivered daylight (glare, distraction, veiling reflections, shadows)
findings.consequent: Visual discomfort, task stimuli, visual performance
findings.quote: Daylight can cause visual discomfort through glare and distraction, and it can diminish the stimuli the task presents to the visual system by producing veiling reflections or by shadows.

findings.antecedent: Daylight causing discomfort or increased task difficulty
findings.consequent: Actions to reduce or eliminate daylight
findings.quote: People will take action to reduce or eliminate daylight if it causes discomfort or increases task difficulty.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to bright light during the day and little/no light at night (daylighting)
findings.consequent: Entrainment of circadian system, performance of visual/non-visual tasks, long-term health problems
findings.quote: Exposure to bright light during the day and little or no light at night will accurately entrain the circadian system. Daylighting is an attractive way to deliver bright light during the day.

findings.antecedent: Different lighting conditions (windows, daylight, view), individual preferences/expectations, habituation
findings.quote: Whether windows will produce an improvement in mood seems to depend on what the individual's preferences and expectations are.

The understanding of how mood influences productivity is weak. Different studies have emphasized worker happiness, well-being, and job satisfaction as predictors of productivity while others have suggested that productivity is itself a generator of feelings of happiness, well-being, and job satisfaction.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to daylight (outdoors, through glass), windows (view), rapid fluctuations in electric light
findings.consequent: Health (tissue damage, Vitamin D, eyestrain, stress, demand for health services, incidence of health problems)
findings.quote: Exposure to daylight can have both positive and negative effects on health. The strongest effects occur outdoors. Exposure to daylight outdoors can cause tissue damage, which is bad, and generate vitamin D, which is good.

findings.consequent: Construction/maintenance costs, building operating costs, rental value
findings.quote: A wall containing windows costs more to construct and maintain than one without. These costs may be offset by reductions in building operating costs. However, the presence of windows is believed to have a positive effect on the rental value of a space.
Daylighting of a conventionally windowless retail space can have a positive effect on sales.

synthesis_conclusions: Daylight is a unique and effective stimulant for human visual and circadian systems, and is psychologically desired, especially when combined with a view.

While daylight can maximize visual performance due to its quantity and spectrum, its effectiveness is highly dependent on proper delivery to avoid discomforts like glare, shadows, and veiling reflections.
People actively manage daylight exposure to avoid discomfort, indicating that good design is crucial for its acceptance and benefits.
Daylight exposure, particularly bright light during the day, is vital for accurate circadian entrainment, which impacts task performance and long-term health.
The link between mood and productivity is weak and complex, with lighting's influence often overshadowed by other factors unless it causes significant discomfort.

Daylight has both positive (Vitamin D production, stress reduction via views, reduced health problems from electric light fluctuations) and negative (tissue damage from UV, eyestrain from poor delivery) health effects.
Windows increase construction and maintenance costs but are believed to positively impact rental value and can offset operating costs through energy savings.
Daylighting in retail spaces can positively affect sales, likely due to an improved visual environment.
evidence_gaps: Reducing the likelihood of discomfort from windows to minimize behaviors that limit daylight admission.
Quantifying the financial return on windows in terms of what people are prepared to pay for them.
Exploring the impact of daylight operating through the circadian system on task performance.
Testing the biophilia hypothesis, particularly the relative importance of a view out versus daylight itself.
Further study on daylighting in schools, including replication of existing findings.
More and better-defined research on the link between environmental satisfaction, job satisfaction, and performance, considering different outcomes like recruitment/retention and cognitive tasks.
limitations: The review explicitly excludes daylight in housing.

The review notes that the understanding of how mood influences productivity is weak, and the influence of lighting is likely overshadowed by many other factors, suggesting limitations in the evidence base for this specific link.
